section_title: What will God plant after the royal vine fails?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 22 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out. I will pluck a tender sprig from its topmost shoots, and I will plant it on a high and lofty mountain. 23 I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel so that it will bear branches; it will yield fruit and become a majestic cedar. Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches. 24 Then all the trees of the field will know that I am the LORD. I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall. I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish. I, the LORD, have spoken, and I have done it.’”

context_lines: The Lord returns to the cedar picture with a promise. This time He Himself takes a tender shoot from its top and plants it on a high mountain in Israel.

The shoot becomes a majestic cedar, bearing branches and fruit, with birds of every kind sheltering beneath it. The failed attempt to secure the kingdom through another eagle is followed by something the Lord establishes Himself.

All the trees will know that He is the Lord. He brings down the tall, raises the low, dries the green and makes the withered flourish. The promise rests on His declared purpose and His power to carry it out.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/17.htm) and [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/17.htm) read the tender royal shoot as the Messiah. Henry identifies Him as Jesus, David’s Son, whose kingdom is established despite what appears small or contemptible at first.

Wesley connects the sheltering birds with the nations finding peace under that rule. Both place the hope beyond Zedekiah’s failed leadership: the Lord Himself supplies the ruler and kingdom in which His purpose succeeds.
god_plan_lines: [Luke 1:30–33](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/1.htm) announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will have no end. That promise explains the larger royal hope to which Christian readers connect Ezekiel’s planted shoot.
[Mark 4:30–34](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/4.htm) gives a close picture of kingdom growth: a small mustard seed becomes a great plant with branches where birds nest in the shade.

Mark does not explicitly quote Ezekiel, and mustard and cedar are different plants. The meaningful parallel is the sheltering kingdom brought from a small beginning. Together, the passages direct hope toward God’s action through Jesus, rather than a ruler’s attempt to manufacture security through a broken pledge.
